newsitem.title: UK: Six IRA men convicted of plot to black out London.
newsitem.headline: Six IRA men convicted of plot to black out London.

text.p: Six IRA men were found guilty on Wednesday of plotting to bomb electricity power stations and paralyse power supplies to London and southeastern England.

The six, some of them described by prosecutors as senior commanders in the Irish Republican Army, were convicted of conspiracy to cause explosions after a three-month trial at London's Old Bailey court. They were to be sentenced later on Wednesday.
The 1996 plot, which police said aimed to cripple London on a scale unseen since World War Two, was thwarted by anti-terrorist officers working undercover with secret service agents.
The defendants had denied the charges, claiming they were planning a hoax to force British authorities to shut down electricity supplies themselves.
During raids on IRA hideouts in the capital, police recovered 37 timers and power units but failed to find explosives.

The prosecution at the trial claimed that six bombs were to be attached to transformers at each of the six power stations ringing London in what the IRA, fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland, intended to be its biggest operation since the end in February 1996 of its 17-month-long ceasefire.
"It was the most sophisticated plan they have ever launched," said anti-terroist police chief Commander John Grieve.

The gang was arrested in London in July last year as it prepared for a dry run. The arrests followed a massive bomb in the northern city of Manchester in June 1996 in which more than 200 people were injured, and a bomb attack in London's Docklands commercial district in February which killed two people and caused millions of pounds worth of damage.
But one of the six, Gerard Hanratty, said the plan was to plant spoof bombs which would bring chaos without endangering life.

"The electrical impact would be total disruption in London. All the traffic lights would be out. It would result in chaos. All industries would be starved -- rail, tube and travel," Hanratty told the court.
The five others convicted were Donald Gannon, 33, Patrick Martin, 34, Robert Morrow, 36, Francis Rafferty, 44 and John Crawley, 39. Two other men were found not guilty of the charges.
